newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwanese mourn teenage school girl's death.
newsitem.headline: Taiwanese mourn teenage school girl's death.

text.p: Thousands of people queued on Sunday to pay their respects to a 17-year-old Taiwanese schoolgirl whose gruesome murder set off a wave of public fury over rising crime on the island.
Government officials and ordinary people crowded into a funeral parlour to bow before a portrait of Pai Hsiao-yen, the daughter of Taiwan actress Pai Ping-ping.
Tearful classmates sang songs and Buddhist monks recited passages from scriptures in the solemn funeral ceremony in Taipei. Pai's body was cremated last week.
"She was only 17. She didn't have enough time to know this world," Pai Ping-ping said in a letter to her daughter, read by a friend at the ceremony.

"I only wish her sacrifice can speak for the public's desire for freedom from fears...If her death can take away all the misfortunes and slightly change the society...then she could say her life had no regret," the letter said.
The nation was shocked when police found the body of Pai, floating naked in a river, on April 28.
Police said her kidnappers had strangled the teenager with two ropes, bound her hands and sunk her in the river with weights. The kidnappers have still not been captured.

They chopped off half the victim's left little finger and sent it to her mother with a demand for US$5 million after snatching her on the way to school on April 14. Her mother wanted to pay, but the kidnappers aborted a planned meeting.
More than 50,000 people marched in Taipei last Sunday to protest against Pai's murder and rising crime. They demanded Premier Lien Chan's resignation and a cabinet reshuffle.
Lien, who has responsibility for domestic affairs, tendered his resignation, but President Lee Teng-hui did not accept it.
Instead he asked Lien to propose some changes in cabinet positions. Three cabinet-level ministers have already resigned.
President Lee apologised for the worsening social order after Pai's murder, the latest in a string of violent crimes that have hit Taiwan since last November.
